draft.title: Natural hazards
card: Bushfires, floods, cyclones and droughts are natural processes. They happen whether or not people are nearby.
A natural process becomes a natural hazard when it threatens people, property or the things people depend on.
The same event can be a hazard in one place and not in another. A flood across empty bushland harms few people. A flood through a town can damage homes and roads.
Hazards differ in how they act. A cyclone brings destructive winds and heavy rain over days. A drought builds slowly over months or years.
draft.remember: A natural process becomes a hazard when it affects people.

a.q: A lightning strike starts a bushfire deep in a national park. No people, homes or farms are near it. How is the fire best described?
opts: A natural process, not yet a hazard
A natural hazard, because it is a fire
A natural hazard, because it burns land
A human-made event, because fire is dangerous
a.why: The fire is a natural process, but it threatens no one. It becomes a hazard only when it affects people or what they depend on. Calling it a hazard just because fires can burn land ignores this.
a.clue: Who or what could the fire harm here?

b.q: Heavy rain floods a wide, empty plain in outback Queensland, and then the same amount of rain floods a town on a river in the north of New South Wales. What does this show?
opts: Hazard depends on how an event affects people
Only the town flood is a natural process
Floods are hazards only when rainfall is very heavy
The plain flood is a hazard because it covers more land
b.why: Both floods are natural processes. Only the town flood affects people and property, so it is the hazard. Size of the area covered does not decide this, as the empty plain harms no one.
b.clue: Both events are natural. What differs is who is in the way.

a.best: A natural process, not yet a hazard

b.best: Hazard depends on how an event affects people
